title: The same two-digit year string lands in a different century depending on which language parses it
assumption: A two-digit year like '68' means the same calendar year no matter which system parses the date string it's embedded in.

input.display: "01/01/68" parsed by Python's strptime("%m/%d/%y") vs JavaScript's legacy Date(string) parser
input.description: A date string with a 2-digit year (common in older CSV exports, legacy forms, and some locale-formatted dates) passed between a Python backend and a JavaScript frontend.

what_goes_wrong: The same string "01/01/68" is read as 2068 by Python and 1968 by Node.js, so a date passed between the two silently moves a century; years 00-49 and 69-99 agree, hiding the bug.
why: Python's strptime with %y follows the POSIX convention: two-digit years 00-68 become 2000-2068 and 69-99 become 1969-1999. V8's legacy (non-ISO) Date parser, used by Node.js and Chrome, pivots at 50 instead: 00-49 become 2000-2049 and 50-99 become 1950-1999. So for the nineteen years 50 through 68 the two runtimes disagree by exactly a century, while every other two-digit year agrees, which is why the bug survives casual testing. ECMA-262 leaves parsing of non-ISO date strings implementation-defined, so other JavaScript engines are free to choose differently again.
fix: Never rely on implicit two-digit-year parsing across a language boundary. Require 4-digit years at every system edge, or, if you must accept 2-digit years, write and apply your own explicit pivot rule identically on both sides.
